title: Lever a crown cap off on a wall-mounted Starr X opener and serve the bottle on a coaster
keywords: bring the workpiece to the tool
instruction: Open the bottle on the mounted bottle opener, then stand the open bottle on the coaster and let go.
context: Bartenders and servers open crown-capped bottles on wall- or cooler-mounted openers, standard bar equipment, many times a shift. The opener is fixed, so the bottle goes to the tool and becomes the lever: tipped well over, its cap goes up into the mouth onto the pad, the lip hooks under the skirt, and pressing the bottle down pries the crimp open. A crown cap can't be pulled or twisted off by hand.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); heights above the table; the layout is the same in every trial. (1) A 275 ml long-neck green glass bottle filled with still water (beer weight, but nothing foams over the rig), 450 g, 18.5 cm tall to the top of its standard 26 mm crown finish: a body 5.8 cm across and 11 cm tall with a cream paper label band, a shoulder narrowing to a lower neck 3.2 cm across (13 to 16.2 cm up), then 2.35 cm under the finish, whose bead is 2.64 cm across and 4.3 mm tall; standing at x 27, y -25. (2) A red 26 mm pry-off steel crown cap crimped on the finish: 2.88 cm across the skirt, 6 mm tall, its skirt's edge 0.7 mm below the bead and 1.2 mm out from it. (3) A Starr X wall-mount bottle opener (Brown Mfg. Co.; zinc-plated cast iron, about 8.3 cm tall, 7 cm wide and 3.2 cm deep; the same pattern is sold as Spill-Stop 13-300), screwed with its two screws (14.9 and 21.3 cm up) to the front of a dark-stained hardwood post 9 cm wide and 2.5 cm deep that stands on the table, clamped to it, its front face at x 41.5, running up to 23.6 cm. The opener is centred on y -20, its mouth facing down and toward the robot; with a cap in the mouth, the middle of the cap's top rests on the opener's fulcrum pad at x 40.0, 17.6 cm up. (4) A cork coaster, 9 cm across and 4 mm thick, centred at x 31, y -4.
scoring: Judged from the video with a ruler. 0 if the bottle ever tilts more than 65 degrees or falls off the table, or if the cap is pried off anywhere but under the opener's prying lip. Otherwise: 1.0 if the opener took the cap off (the lip under the edge of the cap's skirt, inside the opener's mouth, as the cap comes off) and the bottle then stands on the coaster (axis within 3 cm of its centre, base on it, upright within 10 degrees), still (moving under 1 cm/s, turning under 0.5 rad/s) and with no part of either arm (fingers, gripper, wrist or arm) within 1 cm of any part of the bottle (body, shoulder, neck or finish), for 1 s; 0.75 if opened and standing on the coaster but still held, touched (any part of an arm within 1 cm of it) or moving; 0.5 if opened; 0.25 if the lip was under the skirt's edge in the mouth (seen in a second camera filming the mouth from the side; cap axis within 6 mm of the mouth's centre line, seen from the front) but the cap didn't come off; else 0.
reset_notes: The cap is used up: use a new capped bottle, a 275 ml long-neck with a 26 mm crown finish filled with still water and capped with a new 26 mm pry-off crown on a bench crown capper (homebrew suppliers sell all three), and stand it on its mark. Take the popped cap out of the opener's mouth or off the table and throw it away.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (Isaac Sim, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The crimp is a joint: the cap can't slide or turn on the finish and tilts against a spring, letting go once the moment on it reaches 0.9 N m (real 26 mm pry-off crowns: 0.45 to 1.0 N m), its pried edge then 1.5 mm up. A straight pull never opens it (a real crimp holds about 300 N). The skirt is 12 rigid flat segments, not 21 flutes that bend. The opener is boxes: its pad, lip and mouth edge as in its patent drawing. The drink is rigid mass.
